newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ahead 7.3 points in final Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ahead 7.3 points in final Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton led Republican Bob Dole by 7.3 percentage points on Monday in a final Reuters tracking poll that showed overwhelming support from women should give Clinton victory in Tuesday's election.
Clinton led with 44.2 percent to Dole's 36.9 percent in the poll of 1,200 likely voters conducted Friday, Saturday and Sunday by John Zogby Group International, a New York state polling company.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot scored seven percent and 10.4 percent said they were still undecided. The margin of error was plus or minus three percentage points.

Eliminating undecided voters from the survey, the results were: Clinton 49.3 percent, Dole 41.2 percent and Perot 7.8 percent -- a Clinton lead of 8.1 points. The margin of error remained plus or minus three points.
"Many of those undecided voters may not show up at the polls," said pollster John Zogby. "We are probably looking at a Clinton victory with a margin of seven to nine points."
The final day of polling showed a recovery for Clinton and a drop in support for Dole, after the race tightened to less than four points over the weekend.
Other polls predicted a more comfortable Clinton victory, ranging from 10-16 percentage points.

In the battle for control of Congress, the race remained too close to call with Democrats leading by less than a point. However, when asked which party they would like to see controlling the Senate and the House of Representatives, voters expressed a clear preference for Republicans.
In the presidential election, a wide gender gap which emerged early in the race, persisted to the end.

Men preferred Dole by a small margin but Clinton enjoyed a 21-point lead among women, giving him his overall advantage. However, the statistical margin of error in sub-groups within the poll was much higher than for the entire survey.
When respondents were asked whether Clinton deserved a second four-year-term in the White House, 48 percent said he did and 42 percent said he did not.

Voters were almost equally divided when asked whether the country was headed in the right direction or was on the wrong track. Four years ago, a substantial majority said the country was on the wrong track and the incumbent George Bush lost.
Regionally, Clinton held an overwhelming lead in the Northeast but the race remained close in all other parts of the country.
Clinton led among every age group and every income group within the survey. His greatest support was among voters aged 30 or less and senior citizens.
Clinton led overwhelmingly among Catholics, blacks, Jews and Hispanics. Dole led by seven points among Protestants.
